title: Why This Isn't the Dot-Com Bubble | Martin Casado on WSJ's BOLD NAMES

reader_summary.headline: What if everyone who's calling this a bubble has forgotten what a real bubble actually looks like?
reader_summary.overview: What if everyone who's calling this a bubble has forgotten what a real bubble actually looks like? The first live video stream on the internet was a coffee pot. In 1991, a Cambridge researcher pointed a camera at the break room pot so he'd know whether there was coffee before walking downstairs.

key_points.text: People called it a toy, a gimmick with no serious application.
key_points.evidence_quote: People called it a toy, a gimmick with no serious application.

key_points.text: The coffee pot webcam in no small way became Netflix.
key_points.evidence_quote: The coffee pot webcam in no small way became Netflix.

key_points.text: Many major technology waves starts with use cases that look trivial and every time skeptics confuse silliness with insignificance.
key_points.evidence_quote: Many major technology waves starts with use cases that look trivial and every time skeptics confuse silliness with insignificance.

key_points.text: 30 years later, hundreds of billions of dollars are pouring into AI infrastructure.
key_points.evidence_quote: 30 years later, hundreds of billions of dollars are pouring into AI infrastructure.

thesis: The speakers argue that the current influx of hundreds of billions of dollars into AI infrastructure resembles the mobile or cloud booms rather than the dot-com bubble, noting that the dot-com crash was driven by specific factors like a fiber glut, WorldCom's debt and accounting fraud, and 9-11, which are not present today. They suggest that while the current environment feels like a cultural and capital-fueled movement similar to the late 1990s, comparing valuations alone does not predict a systemic collapse.
